You use the present conditional to ask politely (potrebbe…?), express wishes (mi piacerebbe), give advice (dovresti) and make hypotheses (al posto tuo andrei).

To form the regular present conditional: parlerei, prenderei, partirei.
To use the irregular forms (same stem as the future): sarei, avrei, andrei, vorrei.
To ask for something politely: Vorrei…, Potrebbe…?, Le dispiacerebbe…?
To express wishes: Mi piacerebbe…, Avrei voglia di…
To give and ask for advice: Dovresti…, Al posto tuo…, Che cosa faresti?
To make guesses and report unconfirmed news: Secondo il giornale, sarebbe…
The first working day of September. Professor Bellini calls Matei into his office. On the desk there's a letter with the letterhead of the Brukenthal Museum in Sibiu.
Have a seat, Matei. I have a proposal for you. Would you like to go back to Sibiu for a while?
To Sibiu? In what sense, professor?
The Brukenthal Museum and the Uffizi are starting a collaboration. Together we'll restore twelve Italian paintings from their collection.
Italian paintings in Sibiu? I didn't know!
There are quite a few. They'd need a restorer who speaks Romanian and Italian and knows our methods. You'd be perfect.
How long would it be for?
Six months, from January to June. Then you'd come back here on a permanent contract. You'd be my assistant.
Your assistant? Professor, it's… it's an honour. But I'd need to think about it.
Of course. I imagine you'd like to talk it over with Miss Esposito.
Matei, I've been restoring paintings for forty years. I see even the smallest details. Besides, the young lady has been on time since March: that wouldn't be possible without a serious reason.
Would you give me a week to decide?
I'd give you two. But no more: Sibiu is waiting for an answer.
The stress falls on "RE": par-le-REI, po-TRE-sti, vor-REI. "Rei" is one syllable.
Double BB: sa-REB-be, sa-REB-be-ro. Stress on "REB".
Note the difference: VOR-rei (I'd like) ≠ VER-rei (I'd come). Both have a double RR.
The conditional uses the SAME stem as the future (parler-, sar-, avr-, andr-) plus the endings: -ei, -esti, -ebbe, -emmo, -este, -ebbero.
If you know the future, you know the conditional: andrò → andrei, verrò → verrei, potrò → potrei, vorrò → vorrei, berrò → berrei.
Watch out for noi: future "parleremo" (one M), conditional "parleremmo" (MM). You can hear the difference!
The conditional softens requests, just like Romanian ("aș vrea", "ați putea"):
"Le dispiacerebbe…?" = "Would you mind…?" — the most polite formula.
I feel like an ice cream.
Se fossi in te, ci penserei.
If I were you, I'd think about it.
What would you do in my place?
"Se fossi in te" uses the imperfect subjunctive (fossi) — we'll study it later. For now, learn the expression as a block.
The conditional also expresses what would happen in an imaginary situation, or information you don't vouch for (newspaper style):
With a permanent contract, I'd feel more secure.
According to the paper, the museum is supposed to reopen in June.
Without you, what would I do?
The full construction "If I had…, I would…" (Se avessi…, farei…) needs the imperfect subjunctive — we'll learn it at B1 level.
Andrei a Sibiu… ma non so.
Verremmo con te, se ci inviti.
I'd like to live in Naples.
We'd love to come with you.
It would be nice to live in Florence.
"I'd come" or "I'd like": "___ con te." (to come)
Unconfirmed news: "The museum is said to reopen in June."

For three days Matei told no one. He worked, ate little and slept even less. In the end he decided to ask the three people he trusted most for advice.

The first was Graziella. He found her in the kitchen at six in the morning, kneading bread. "What would you do in my place?" he asked her. She didn't stop kneading. "Me? I would never leave Florence. But I'm seventy-three and I have a trattoria. You're thirty and you have a trade you can practise anywhere in the world."
"So I should go?" "So you should do what makes your heart beat. Six months go by fast. I'll be here, the trattoria will be here, and your room will be here. I wouldn't give it to anyone else."

The second was Pietro, who had become very wise since turning nine. "If you went to Sibiu, could I come and visit you?" he asked straight away. "Of course." "And would there be snow?" "Loads." "Then go. But you should bring me a Romanian present every month. And you should phone me on Saturdays."

The third piece of advice he asked for on the phone. His mother answered on the first ring, as always. Matei explained everything. She was silent for a moment. Then she said: "My son, I'd be overjoyed to have you home for six months. I'd cook you everything you miss. But I'd never ask it of you if you had to leave something important behind in Florence."
"Something or someone?" Matei asked. "You know better than I do," she answered. "Have you talked to Giulia yet?" Matei closed his eyes. That was exactly what he hadn't yet found the courage to do.

That evening he climbed the four floors on via della Chiesa with heavy legs. Giulia was on the terrace with a glass of wine and a book she wasn't reading. "At last," she said, without turning round. "Bellini told me three days ago. I was waiting for you to tell me."
Matei sat down next to her. "I wouldn't want to leave without you," he said. "Six months would be too long."

Giulia smiled and took a letter out of her bag. It had the same Brukenthal Museum letterhead. "Bellini is a clever man," she said. "He wrote to Sibiu that they'd need two restorers, not one. And guess who the second would be?"
Matei looked at her, speechless. "You'd come with me? Six months at minus fifteen? You, who feel cold at eighteen?"

"I'd come with you to Siberia," Giulia replied. "But in Sibiu there's your mother who cooks, and your father who's already taught me to say 'noroc'. It would be silly to say no." Then she raised her glass. "If I were you, I'd accept. No — if I were us."
The next day Matei walked into Bellini's office at eight sharp. "I accept, professor. We accept." Bellini looked up from his papers and, for the second time in a year, said: "Bene."
